drafts.walkScript: Start at line 1. The lane goes up-hill, and she stops at the middle. Line 1 says she 'sat down on' a stile. Line 2 says the stile 'led thence into a field'. She is on the stile, not in the field.

Read lines 13 and 14 as one sentence about Mrs Umney. Line 14 says the request was 'Lady Canterville's earnest request'. Line 14 then says Mrs Otis 'had consented to keep' her on. So Lady Canterville asked, and Mrs Otis agreed. Nothing in these lines says Mrs Umney had nowhere else to go.

Look at lines 22 and 23, where Mrs Otis speaks. She says 'something has been spilt there'. Her words before that are a polite way of speaking, not fear. Line 22 says she did not know 'what it really signified'. Mrs Umney names Lady Eleanore later, on line 29, not Mrs Otis.

Line 16 has Maggie guess 'the tipsy-cake'. On line 18 Tom says 'No', so the cake is not his reason. Then he says 'It's the pudden', which means the pudding. Line 19 names that pudding: 'apricot roll-up'. Tom names the roll-up himself, and Maggie never guesses it.

Line 2 says Jim thought he 'should like an apple'. The very next words are 'ran on deck'. So the apple is the reason he went up. Line 1 says his work was over, but that only sets the time. On line 2 it is 'The watch', not Jim, looking out for the island.

Line 18 ends with 'behind the peaceful and sunlit countryside'. Line 19 says what 'rose ever' there. It is 'the long, gloomy curve of the moor'. The 'old gabled houses' on line 17 are part of the countryside itself.

Line 58 reaches the gates. Line 59 gives 'pillars on either side, blotched with lichens'. The words 'surmounted by' on line 59 mean topped by. Line 60 says what topped them: the 'boars’ heads of the Baskervilles'. The iron tracery on line 58 belongs to the gates, not the pillar tops.

Find 'herself literary' at the start of line 8. Line 6 says she thought this 'on the strength' of some things. Line 7 names them: 'manuscript sermons' and 'a pretty good library of divinity'. So the sermons and divinity books are why she felt literary. Being a rector's daughter on line 6 is who she was, not the reason given.

On line 18 Captain Brown begins, and on line 19 she cuts in. Line 20 has him ask to 'read you a scene out of this month's number'. Line 21 adds that he had it 'only this morning'. He thinks 'the company' cannot have read it yet. His words on line 18 are a remark, not the thing he asks to do.
